Trump vs Xi Jinping: The winner shapes the next century of technology.

In April 2024, Biden signed an act giving Tiktok owner ByteDance 270 days to sell or face a complete ban in the U.S.

ByteDance's Beijing roots and data collection practices were cited as primary concerns.

But the path to that point was far from linear:

Trump tried to ban TikTok outright in 2020, but courts blocked it.

Then Biden's administration pivoted to a divestiture approach, citing national security.

Congress acted with unusual speed.

But here's the core faultline:

National Security vs Free Speech.

Government officials claim TikTok's data collection and algorithm could facilitate Chinese espionage.

Critics argue it's censorship, stomping on the First Amendment rights of 170M Americans.

Enter the courts, once again:

What happens to TikTok USA under new ownership?  Will it thrive or stumble?

China's algorithm export rules mean the secret sauce stays behind.

Add a 50% US stake, and it's a weird hybrid entity - and the implications extend far beyond TikTok itself:

It has set the precedent for more forced divestitures under the umbrella of "national security."

It has undoubtedly escalated the 21st-century battle for dominance between the US and China.

Here's what to expect:

TikTok USA will initially save its 170M user base under new ownership.

But without its core algorithm, it will lose stickiness over time - opening the door for Meta, Snapchat, and X.

If Amazon acquires it, it'll likely become an adjunct to Prime.

But the stakes go higher:

Fundamentally, we're navigating a new era:

• Regulation vs. innovation
• Nationalism vs. globalism
• Free markets and antitrust
• Public vs. private sector interests
• Product experience vs. data privacy
• National security vs. free expression

It's a messy, evolving issue with significant consequences - small and large.

Only time will tell how this chapter in digital governance concludes.
